importance_ranking.reason: Buyers scan listing images to immediately identify building type (warehouse vs factory vs cold storage), structural form (clear-span PEB vs truss shed vs modular), and visual scale — wrong type or form is an instant skip. High visual variation across sub-types means image is the fastest qualification signal before any text is read.

Clear-span width, eave height, crane capacity, and service type (turnkey vs structure-only) are primary shortlisting gates — a buyer with a 30 ft eave height and 10-ton crane requirement cannot evaluate a listing that omits these. Specs drive the shortlist before price is considered.

importance_ranking.brand_important_reason: Recognised national PEB brands — Kirby, Interarch, Everest Industries, Zamil Steel, EPACK, Tata BlueScope — are actively searched by name by institutional and EPC buyers who treat brand as a proxy for engineering capability, IS-code compliance, and post-erection service.
importance_ranking.reason: This is a high-value, site-engineered, turnkey capital purchase — institutional buyers (EPC contractors, logistics operators, government PSUs) evaluate manufacturer credentials, IS 800/IS 2062 compliance track record, and erection capability as part of vendor qualification, often before finalising price. Seller identity is a primary trust signal, not a post-shortlist check.

Every PEB project is custom-engineered to site-specific load requirements (wind zone, seismic zone, crane loads, span), so no fixed list price exists — listed prices are indicative per-sq-ft rates used as budget entry points. Indian buyers are price-aggressive but final price is always negotiated after spec confirmation; price is a sanity-check signal, not a primary shortlisting lever.

importance_ranking.unit_note: Sellers quote in per sq ft (standard structures), per project lump sum (turnkey custom builds), or per MT (steel supply only) — these are not interchangeable and create real price comparison confusion. Per sq ft is the dominant buyer comparison unit; listings must show unit alongside any indicative price to prevent misreading.
importance_ranking.reason: Unit ambiguity is a genuine market problem in this category — per sq ft vs per project vs per MT represent fundamentally different commercial scopes, and a buyer comparing indicative prices without unit clarity will misread cost by an order of magnitude.

top_configurator_specs.reason: Defines what the building IS — Factory, Warehouse, Cold Storage, Workshop, Shed are non-interchangeable use-case classes with fundamentally different structural, insulation, and compliance requirements, driving the largest price and design variation across the product range.

Crane provision (none vs 5T vs 10T vs 20T) drives primary frame sizing, column spacing, and haunch design — a building with a 20-ton overhead crane requires significantly heavier and more expensive primary steel than a no-crane warehouse of identical footprint, making this the dominant within-type price configurator.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Clear-span width (e.g., 15 m, 24 m, 30 m, 40 m) is the primary structural design driver — it determines primary frame weight, column-free floor area, and cost per sq ft, and buyers specify it as a non-negotiable project requirement before any other dimension.

Indian PEB structures must be designed to site-specific wind and seismic zone loads per IS 875 and IS 1893 — buyers in high-wind coastal zones or seismic zones III/IV require explicit compliance confirmation, and this materially affects steel tonnage and cost.

Bay length (spacing between primary frames, typically 6–9 m) determines purlin and secondary member sizing and directly affects total steel tonnage and cost — buyers with specific equipment layout or column-spacing requirements specify this as a project constraint.

top_rfq_specs.reason: Application (Factory, Warehouse, Cold Storage, Rice Mill, etc.) immediately routes the RFQ to sellers with the right structural and compliance capability — a cold storage application requires insulated PUF panel construction that most standard PEB fabricators cannot supply, while a factory with heavy machinery requires crane provisions.

Eave height (10 ft to 35 ft) determines primary frame design, crane compatibility, and structural steel tonnage — sellers need this to assess whether they can supply the required structure and to provide an accurate indicative price.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Clear-span width is the single most important structural parameter sellers need to assess feasibility and price — it drives primary frame design, steel tonnage, and cost per sq ft, and cannot be inferred from total area or height alone.

Whether the buyer needs an overhead crane (and at what capacity) fundamentally changes the structural design and cost — sellers cannot quote accurately without knowing this, and buyers with crane requirements will receive irrelevant responses from sellers who only supply standard warehouse structures.
